title: A cue switches on a ring of relay cells

trials.label: light from the left, no cue
light from the left, cue first
light from the right, no cue
light from the right, cue first

mechanism: This 49-cell body grew a closed band of 27 relay cells (type A on the page) around a small middle; the other 22 cells are slow light-sensing cells (type B): 13 sit around the outside of the band, and 9 fill the middle, where the light is never strong enough to make them fire. With no cue, only 1-3 of the outside type-B cells on the brightest edge charge up enough to fire, 5-8 ticks after the light comes on, so the body points at the light with about 2 spikes. A resting relay cell sits halfway to firing, so the cue spot sets off the relay cells under it, and a single spike from a relay neighbour is enough to set off the next one: the signal spreads along the band one cell per tick, until all 27 are firing 6-8 ticks later, as far as 4-5 sites from the spot. From then on the whole band stays switched on, every relay cell firing on every tick and re-lighting its neighbours, for as long as the dark wait lasts; that steady 'on' state is the memory, and if it is silenced for even one tick it never comes back. While it is on, the relay spikes keep pushing down the charge of the type-B cells next to them, holding it near -17 when firing takes +1, so when the light comes on they are still much too low to fire before scoring ends. Light switches relay cells off: the bright half of the band goes quiet within one tick, and the quiet then creeps toward the dark side over the next 3-6 ticks as each relay cell loses the neighbours that kept it going; scoring starts 3 ticks after the light, so it catches the end of that fade, all on the dark side, and the body faces away.
evidence: Organism: outputs/context_lattice/hex_sex_s1, picked over lattice hex_sex_s0/s2 and evo hex_sex_s0/s2 (lattice s2 scores higher held-out, 0.89, but shuffling its cell types only drops it to 0.56-0.62). Run log: held-out 0.81, messages off 0.00, types shuffled 0.24, best single type 0.41; on fresh 48-trial held-out sets 0.89-0.93, shuffled 0.29-0.30. Rule edits on 96 held-out trials (0.89 unchanged; 0.93 uncued, 0.85 cued): relay cells can't sense the cue, 0.00 (cued trials -0.93, the body just faces the light); relay cells ignore each other, 0.00; relay cells can't sense light, 0.44 (the band stays on evenly on both sides, cued -0.04); type B can't sense the cue, no change; type B ignores all incoming spikes, cued trials fall to 0.25-0.27 (4 held-out sets), and ignoring only relay spikes gives 0.32-0.34, because the bright-side type-B spikes come back. The memory, on 240 held-out trials: in all 113 cued trials where a relay cell is under the cue, a relay cell's first spike comes exactly as many ticks after the cue as it is steps along the band from the spot (0-8), the band is full 6-8 ticks after the cue starts, and from then on all 27 relay cells fire on every tick until the light comes on. A relay cell with a firing relay neighbour fired on the next tick in 47274 of 47274 dark-wait cases. Silencing the band for one tick just before the light: it never restarts, cued -0.05 (no scored spikes); 10 ticks before: cued -0.89 (the type-B cells have recovered and the body faces the light). Adding 80 or 300 extra dark ticks before the light leaves the shown cued twins' scores unchanged (0.85, 0.94), with all 27 relay cells still firing. Nothing circles and the closed loop is not needed: cutting the band at any of 4 places (2-3 relay cells removed, so it no longer encloses the middle) leaves every remaining relay cell firing at light-on in every cued trial where the cue touched one, and two relay cells on their own keep each other going indefinitely, taking turns. Cuts lower cued scores (0.82 to 0.47-0.61) only by shortening the scored dark-side tail. If relay cells had to rest one tick after each spike, the memory still holds (12-15 of 27 firing at light-on) but the dark side dies within a tick of the light and cued trials fall to -0.05. The fade after light-on (mean relay cells firing per tick, cued trials): bright half 13.5 just before, then 1.8, then 0; dark half 13.5, then 11.3, 10.0, 7.1, 4.9, 2.7, 1.4, 0.4, 0 over ticks 0-7. Relay cells nearer the light stop sooner (correlation -0.77 between position toward the light and last firing tick). 100% of scored cued spikes are on the dark half. The brake: bright-edge type-B charge in cued trials is -17.4 at the end of the dark wait and -9.2 just before scoring (uncued: 0 and +0.6). Even unbraked, these cells need 5-8 ticks of light to fire, and scoring runs from 3 to 10 ticks after light-on, so a small push down is enough: type B ignoring incoming spikes only during the dark wait, or only after light-on, changes nothing (cued 0.82). Who does what: of the 22 type-B cells, the 9 in the middle never fire in 240 trials, and removing them (cued 0.823 vs 0.820) or turning them into relay cells (0.831) changes nothing; 10 of the 13 outside ones fire at some point, and each touches 2-3 relay cells. All cells relay: uncued 0.00, cued 0.82. All cells type B: uncued 0.93, cued -0.93. Outside type B removed: uncued 0.00, cued 0.87. Uncued trials score with 1-3 spikes (70 of 120 have 2), each from a different outside type-B cell; cued trials average 9 scored spikes, all from relay cells, and about 435 spikes in total. Shown trials: held-out pool of 24 (seed 0), trials 5, 17, 1, 13; light from -165 degrees (left, a little from below) and 15 degrees (right, a little from above). Each twin has the same light field, timing and scoring window. Scores: left 0.93 uncued / 0.85 cued, right 0.91 / 0.94; with messages off the cued twins score -0.93 / -0.90.
